overview: The Jetson Orin Nano shares the older Jetson Nano's basic idea — a small board with a real GPU for running neural networks locally — but the GPU generation gap is enormous: the original Nano's 128-core Maxwell GPU tops out around half a TFLOP of compute with no dedicated tensor hardware, while the Orin Nano's Ampere GPU adds dedicated Tensor Cores and reaches tens of TOPS of INT8 inference performance, roughly a 20x class jump that's the difference between running one lightweight model at a few frames per second and running multiple real-time vision models (or a compact vision-language model) simultaneously on the same board. That extra headroom is why it shows up in newer autonomous mobile robots and drones doing real-time multi-camera perception rather than a single low-res detector. Like its predecessor it still ships with no built-in WiFi and uses physical/'BOARD' pin numbering rather than Raspberry Pi-style BCM numbering in its GPIO library, but it adds an M.2 NVMe slot that most serious deployments use instead of booting a full JetPack + CUDA + ML-framework stack off a microSD card, which is both slower and wears the card out faster under heavy write load.
simpleSummary: A small, more powerful successor to the Jetson Nano with a much stronger built-in GPU, made for running real-time AI vision on a robot.

specifications.gpu: 1024-core NVIDIA Ampere GPU with 32 Tensor Cores
specifications.aiPerformance: up to ~67 TOPS INT8 (highest power mode) — roughly 20x the original Jetson Nano's Maxwell GPU
specifications.storage: microSD card, plus an M.2 Key M slot for a NVMe SSD
specifications.connectivity: Gigabit Ethernet (no built-in WiFi — needs a USB dongle or M.2 Key E card)
specifications.power: 7-25W configurable power modes via barrel jack or USB-C PD

pinMap.name: Pin 2 (5V)
pinMap.function: 5V rail sourced from the board's power input.
pinMap.currentLimit: Depends on supply headroom and active power mode

pinMap.name: Pin 6 (GND)
pinMap.function: Common ground reference for the header.

pinMap.name: Pin 3 (I2C SDA)
pinMap.function: Default I2C data line for connecting sensors or displays.
pinMap.gotcha: Jetson.GPIO addresses this header by physical pin number (BOARD mode) by default, not by a Pi-style GPIO/BCM number — copy-pasting a Raspberry Pi pin number here usually addresses the wrong pin.

pinMap.name: Pin 32 (PWM)
pinMap.function: General-purpose I/O, PWM capable — commonly used for a cooling fan or servo.

pinMap.name: USB-C Power Input
pinMap.function: USB-C port usable for board power delivery (in addition to or instead of the barrel jack, depending on carrier board).
pinMap.currentLimit: Up to 3A depending on power mode
pinMap.gotcha: Not every USB-C cable/charger supplies enough wattage. A low-power phone-charger cable can brownout or throttle the board the moment the GPU ramps up under an inference load.

pinMap.name: DisplayPort Output
pinMap.function: Video output for connecting a monitor directly to the board for local development.

pinMap.name: CSI Camera Port 1
pinMap.function: MIPI CSI-2 camera connector, first of two available.
pinMap.gotcha: Using both CSI ports for a stereo rig requires the camera driver/device tree to actually support dual-camera capture — some third-party CSI camera modules only ship a single-camera driver.

pinMap.name: CSI Camera Port 2
pinMap.function: MIPI CSI-2 camera connector, second of two available.

pinMap.name: M.2 NVMe Slot
pinMap.function: M.2 Key M slot for an NVMe SSD, used to boot the OS instead of (or in addition to) microSD.
pinMap.gotcha: A full JetPack + CUDA + ML framework install routinely exceeds what a microSD card handles well in terms of both speed and write endurance — most serious projects move the OS to an NVMe SSD here fairly early.

pinMap.name: Ethernet Port
pinMap.function: Gigabit Ethernet jack, the primary wired network connection since there's no built-in WiFi.
pinMap.gotcha: There is no built-in WiFi — a robot design that assumes wireless connectivity out of the box needs a USB WiFi dongle or an M.2 Key E card added explicitly.

useCases.title: Real-time multi-camera object detection and tracking
useCases.scenario: Run several lightweight detection models across multiple camera feeds simultaneously on a mobile robot, something the original Jetson Nano's GPU couldn't keep up with in real time.

useCases.title: On-device vision-language perception
useCases.scenario: Run a compact vision-language or multimodal model directly on the board for a robot to interpret scenes in natural-language terms without a cloud round trip.

useCases.title: SLAM with semantic segmentation
useCases.scenario: Combine simultaneous localization and mapping with real-time semantic segmentation for a mobile robot navigating cluttered indoor spaces.

useCases.title: Onboard drone vision compute
useCases.scenario: Serve as the flight computer's companion vision board, running obstacle detection and visual odometry onboard a drone.

useCases.title: Teaching CUDA/TensorRT deployment pipelines
useCases.scenario: Use the board in a robotics course to teach students how to optimize and deploy trained models with TensorRT for real-time inference on embedded hardware.

commonlyPairedWith: Microcontroller as a real-time motor-control co-processor
oftenConfusedWith: Jetson Nano (older, far less AI compute — no Tensor Cores, a fraction of the TOPS)
Raspberry Pi 4/5 with a Coral USB accelerator (external accelerator bolted on, rather than an integrated GPU)
oftenUpgradedTo: Jetson AGX Orin (substantially higher power budget and performance for industrial-tier deployments)

beginnerMistakes: Running the board in a low power mode and then being surprised inference is slower than the advertised peak TOPS figure.
Booting and running heavy AI workloads from a microSD card instead of moving to the M.2 NVMe slot, hitting both a speed wall and premature card wear.
Assuming built-in WiFi like a typical dev board — it needs a USB dongle or M.2 WiFi card.
Copy-pasting Raspberry Pi GPIO pin numbers directly into Jetson.GPIO code instead of using the board's physical/BOARD numbering.
Powering the board from a low-wattage USB-C phone charger cable and seeing it throttle or brown out under GPU load.
